articles.title: Who decides how tax money reaches the states?
articles.subject: Polity & Economy
articles.excerpt: Two different decisions determine how a common tax pool reaches an individual state.

sections.heading: Start with a school
paragraphs: A government school needs teachers, classrooms and money every year. The state pays for much of this work, while the Union collects several major taxes. The practical question is how revenue collected at one level helps pay for responsibilities at another.

Article 280 provides for a Finance Commission, constituted by the President every five years or earlier if necessary. Among its tasks is recommending how the net proceeds of shareable Union taxes should be distributed. It recommends a framework; it does not send a separate payment to every school.

sections.heading: Follow the money through two decisions
paragraphs: First decide how much of the divisible pool goes to the states collectively. This is vertical devolution. Then divide that states’ share among individual states. This is horizontal devolution. A percentage is incomplete until you know which of those pools it describes.

The horizontal formula addresses differences between states: their capacity to raise revenue, the population they serve and other criteria used in the relevant award. Equal percentages are not the same as equal resources or equal ability to provide services. Check the actual recommendation before naming its criteria or weights.

sections.heading: A tax share is not a grant
paragraphs: Tax devolution shares revenue through the award’s distribution framework. A grant is a separate transfer with its own purpose and applicable conditions. Combining the two under a single headline can hide whether a state gained a larger share, received a particular grant, or simply benefited from a growing tax pool.

When comparing states, use the same financial year and distinguish recommended amounts from money actually transferred. Also check the award period and implementation documents. The durable idea is fiscal federalism: revenue and spending responsibilities sit at different levels, so transfers help connect them.

articles.takeaway: A state’s percentage and its rupee receipts answer different questions. Identify the pool, period and type of transfer before comparing them.
articles.question: A state’s horizontal share falls from 15% to 12%, while the states’ pool rises from ₹40 to ₹50. Has its tax receipt fallen? These figures are illustrative.

sources.label: Constitution of India · Articles 270 and 280
sources.note: Start with Article 280(3)(a), which distinguishes distribution between the Union and states from allocation between states. Article 270 concerns the divisible pool.

sources.label: Finance Commission · reports and recommendations
sources.note: Open the report for the award period being discussed. Read the tax-devolution formula and grants separately; a homepage alone does not establish a current percentage.

example.heading: The percentage changed. Did the money?
example.text: Suppose the divisible pool is ₹100, the states together receive ₹40, and State A receives ₹6. These numbers are illustrative. State A has 15% of the states’ pool but 6% of the original pool. If the states’ pool later becomes ₹50 and State A still receives ₹6, its horizontal share falls to 12%. Its rupee amount has not fallen. Always check the denominator.

comparison.heading: Share, allocation and grant
rows: Vertical devolution
How much of the divisible pool goes to the states together?
Horizontal devolution
How is that states’ share divided between individual states?
Grant
What additional assistance is recommended, and for what purpose?

articles.recallAnswer: No: 15% of ₹40 and 12% of ₹50 are both ₹6. The percentage fell, but the amount stayed the same. You would still need comparable periods and implementation evidence before drawing a conclusion about real state finances.

articles.title: The repo rate changed. Why hasn’t your loan?
articles.subject: Economy
articles.excerpt: A policy decision reaches your loan through its benchmark, spread and next reset date.

sections.heading: Start with the loan agreement
paragraphs: A repo-rate decision makes headlines, but your loan instalment stays unchanged. That alone does not show that the decision had no effect. The first useful document is your loan agreement: which benchmark does it name, what spread is added, and when does the interest rate reset?

The policy repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against eligible collateral under its repo operations. Your bank’s lending rate is a different rate. Funding costs, the benchmark and the contract determine how a policy change can reach a particular borrower.

For a dated example, the MPC resolution of 7 October 2026 records a 25-basis-point increase in the policy repo rate to 5.50%. That establishes the policy decision at that meeting. It does not establish what happened to a particular borrower’s loan; the contract and repayment schedule are still needed.

sections.heading: Three links, not one automatic change
paragraphs: For a loan priced as a benchmark plus a spread, a lower benchmark can reduce the borrower’s rate when the applicable reset occurs. The spread is the amount added to that benchmark. Read the contract before assuming that either component changes immediately or by the same amount as the policy rate.

Different loans can respond differently. An externally benchmarked floating-rate loan, one tied to an internal bank benchmark and a fixed-rate loan do not follow identical arrangements. A fixed rate does not ordinarily change merely because the repo rate changed.

sections.heading: An unchanged instalment can hide a change
paragraphs: Even after the interest rate falls, the monthly instalment may stay the same if the repayment tenure changes instead. Check the rate notice and repayment schedule, not just the amount debited from your account. The available choices and timing depend on the loan’s terms and applicable rules.

This is monetary transmission: a central-bank decision affects funding and lending conditions, which can influence borrowing, spending and prices. The chain takes time and can weaken at several points. A borrower’s experience is one part of that chain, not a complete measure of economy-wide transmission.

articles.takeaway: To judge a loan’s response, follow the benchmark, spread, reset date and repayment schedule.
articles.question: The loan rate has fallen but the monthly debit is unchanged. What would you inspect before concluding that the borrower received no benefit?

sources.label: RBI · MPC resolution · 7 October 2026
sources.note: Read “Monetary Policy Decisions”, paragraphs 1–2, for the meeting dates and actual decision. The loan figures used in the worked illustration are hypothetical, not the policy rates in this release.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India · frequently asked questions
sources.note: Use the relevant explanation of lending benchmarks and floating rates, then compare it with the actual loan agreement. A general FAQ index is a starting point.

example.heading: Read the next reset, then the repayment schedule
example.text: Imagine a loan with a 6% benchmark and a 2% spread. Its rate is 8%. If the benchmark becomes 5.75% and the spread stays unchanged, the rate becomes 7.75% at the applicable reset. These are illustrative figures, not current RBI rates. The lender might reduce the instalment or adjust the tenure under the agreement; the rate and repayment schedule reveal what happened.

comparison.heading: Read the right rate
rows: Policy repo rate
The RBI’s policy decision and effective date.
Loan benchmark
The benchmark named in this particular contract.
Borrower’s rate
Benchmark plus spread, subject to the contract and reset schedule.

articles.recallAnswer: Compare the outstanding balance and repayment schedule, including the remaining tenure, as well as the rate and its effective date. A shorter tenure can reflect lower interest costs even when the instalment stays unchanged. Check the contract rather than assuming this happens for every loan.

articles.title: A wetland is more than a place on a list
articles.subject: Environment
articles.excerpt: A wetland’s boundary tells you where it is. Water flows help explain whether it can function.

sections.heading: Begin with the water
paragraphs: Picture a low-lying area that holds water after rain. Depending on its ecology, it can slow runoff, support habitat and sustain local livelihoods. Filling it, polluting its inflow or interrupting a channel can change what happens during the next wet season.

Wetlands are varied. The Convention on Wetlands covers a broad range of ecosystems, including marshes, lakes and coastal areas. They are not all freshwater, permanently flooded or untouched by people. A list of names tells you much less than an explanation of how one site receives and releases water.

sections.heading: Designation and condition are different questions
paragraphs: A Ramsar designation identifies a wetland as internationally important under the Convention. It does not, by itself, demonstrate that the site is healthy today. Its present condition needs dated evidence about water, habitat, pollution and other pressures.

The Convention’s idea of wise use concerns maintaining ecological character through ecosystem approaches within sustainable development. It is not a blanket ban on every human activity. The question is how a use affects the ecosystem’s functioning and the people who depend on it.

sections.heading: Look beyond the line on the map
paragraphs: Water can arrive from outside the designated boundary. A catchment is the surrounding area that drains towards a water body. Development upstream can therefore affect a wetland even when no one builds inside it. Examine inflows, outflows and seasonal timing before attributing a change to one cause.

For a real site, start with its Ramsar Information Sheet: location, wetland type, hydrology, ecological features and reported pressures. Then check the record’s update date and look for current monitoring. An older description is useful background, but it cannot establish the site’s condition this year.

articles.takeaway: Understand the wetland as a connected water system. Its designation, ecological description and current condition require different evidence.
articles.question: A wetland remains within its protected boundary, but fish breeding declines after construction upstream. Does the unchanged boundary rule out a conservation problem?

sources.label: Convention on Wetlands · convention and wise use
sources.note: Find the Convention text: Article 1.1 defines wetlands, while Article 3.1 addresses conservation and wise use. Read wise-use guidance before equating it with a ban on use.

sources.label: Ramsar Sites Information Service · individual site records
sources.note: Search an individual site and read its Ramsar Information Sheet, including hydrology, ecological features and reported pressures. Check when the record was updated.

example.heading: A road outside the boundary
example.text: Imagine a raised road crossing a channel that brings seasonal runoff into a wetland. The wetland itself is not filled, yet its inflow may change. This is a hypothetical example, not a documented claim about a Ramsar site. To investigate it, compare water movement before and after construction, seasonal rainfall and habitat changes. The map should include the catchment, not just the protected boundary.

comparison.heading: Designation and condition
rows: Is it internationally designated?
The Ramsar designation and site record.
What kind of wetland is it?
Its habitat, hydrology and ecological description.
Is it healthy now?
Dated monitoring evidence, pressures and changes in ecological character.

articles.recallAnswer: No. A boundary does not capture every connection to the catchment. Investigate water flow, seasonal timing, habitat and other possible causes using dated evidence. The timing of construction is a reason to investigate, not proof that it caused the decline.

articles.title: A Bill passed. Is the new rule in force?
articles.subject: Polity
articles.excerpt: Parliamentary passage, presidential assent and commencement are separate steps. Check which one the headline reports.

sections.heading: Passed does not settle the effective date
paragraphs: A headline says Parliament has passed a Bill. Someone forwards it as proof that a new requirement applies tomorrow. That conclusion skips two questions: has the Bill received presidential assent, and has the relevant provision come into force?

For an ordinary Bill, passage through Parliament and presidential assent are distinct stages in becoming an Act. Articles 107–111 provide the constitutional framework. Money Bills and constitutional amendments have different procedures, so first identify the kind of Bill you are reading about.

sections.heading: Read the commencement provision
paragraphs: An Act may take effect immediately, on a specified date, or on a date appointed through a notification. Its own commencement provision tells you which route applies. Some Acts allow different provisions to start on different dates; the title of the Act alone cannot resolve that.

Where a notification appoints a date, read the notification alongside the relevant section. Assent establishes one legal milestone; commencement establishes when the specified provision operates. A press release summarising the legislation is a useful lead, but the enacted text and notification answer the legal question.

sections.heading: Then check the rules and the actual obligation
paragraphs: Rules can supply procedures needed to operate a provision: an application form, an authority, a deadline or a reporting process. Do not assume that every section waits for every rule, or that publication of any rules starts the entire Act. Read the specific provisions together.

A useful legal note therefore records four things: the Act and section, its commencement mechanism, the applicable notification and date, and any relevant rules. This separates an announcement from an operative requirement. If one document is missing, state the gap rather than guessing when the obligation begins.

articles.takeaway: Follow the specific provision from enacted text to commencement and applicable rules before describing a legal duty as active.
articles.question: A Bill has received assent, but its reporting-duty section starts on a date to be notified. You have not found that notification. What can you safely conclude?

sources.label: Constitution of India · Articles 107–111
sources.note: Articles 107–111 set out parts of the Union legislative process. Money Bills have a distinct procedure; avoid applying one ordinary-Bill shorthand to every Bill.

sources.label: India Code · Acts and subordinate legislation
sources.note: Open the particular Act. Read its commencement section, then any commencement notifications and relevant rules. An Act’s presence in the database alone does not prove that every provision is in force.

example.heading: One Act, two starting dates
example.text: Imagine an Act that allows the government to appoint different commencement dates. A notification brings sections 1–5 into force on 1 June, while section 8 is not included. These details are hypothetical. If section 8 contains the new reporting duty, that notification alone does not show the duty is operative. Check for a later notification and any provisions relevant to the duty.

comparison.heading: Three documents, three checks
rows: Passage
The legislative record showing approval through the applicable procedure.
Assent
The enacted law and assent/publication record.
Commencement
The Act’s start-date clause and any notification it requires.

articles.recallAnswer: You can say the Bill became an Act after assent. You cannot establish that this reporting duty is in force from assent alone. Search the official notifications and identify the section and effective date before making that stronger claim.

articles.title: When GDP grows, how much is just higher prices?
articles.subject: Economy
articles.excerpt: A bigger money total can reflect more output, higher prices, or both. The price basis makes the difference.

sections.heading: Begin with ten loaves
paragraphs: A bakery sells ten loaves for ₹20 each, then sells the same ten loaves for ₹25 each. Its sales value rises from ₹200 to ₹250, although the number of loaves does not change. These illustrative figures show why a larger money total need not mean more goods.

GDP measures value added in production across the economy, rather than simply adding every business’s sales. Current-price, or nominal, GDP uses prices of the period being measured. Changes in that value can reflect output and prices together.

sections.heading: Keep the price basis consistent
paragraphs: Constant-price, or real, GDP estimates aim to separate changes in production from price changes using the statistical framework and its reference prices. This makes real growth a better starting point when asking whether output increased. It is not calculated by simply subtracting a familiar retail inflation rate from nominal growth.

A GDP deflator relates nominal and real GDP; the Consumer Price Index measures prices for a consumer basket. Their coverage and construction differ. Also check the base year, whether a figure is quarterly or annual, and whether the release revises an earlier estimate.

sections.heading: Growth needs a denominator and a second question
paragraphs: A growth rate compares a level with another period’s level. A weak comparison period can make a later increase look particularly large: this is a base effect. Read the underlying levels and compare like periods rather than treating a single percentage as the whole story.

GDP also does not tell you how gains are distributed. Aggregate growth, growth per person, household incomes and employment answer different questions. Once the output and price distinction is clear, ask who benefited and what additional evidence is needed.

articles.takeaway: Identify the period and price basis, then separate output growth from questions about living standards and distribution.
articles.question: The value of output rises 21%, while output measured at the original prices rises 10%. Can you say retail inflation was 11%?

sources.label: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation · national accounts
sources.note: Go to National Accounts and open the dated estimate release being quoted. Check current versus constant prices, the base year, the comparison period and whether the estimate was revised.

example.heading: More output and higher prices at the same time
example.text: Suppose a simple economy produces 100 identical items at ₹10 each: ₹1,000. Next period it produces 110 at ₹11 each: ₹1,210. At the original price, the second period’s output is worth ₹1,100. In this illustration, money value rises 21% while quantity rises 10%. Actual national accounts cover many products and value added; this fixed-product example only isolates the two effects.

comparison.heading: Do not swap these measures
rows: GDP at current prices
Changes in money value, including price changes.
GDP at constant prices
Output changes measured using a common price basis.
GDP per person
Aggregate output relative to population, without describing its distribution.

articles.recallAnswer: No. In the illustration, the price ratio is 1.21 ÷ 1.10 = 1.10, a 10% increase. Growth effects compound rather than add. More broadly, a GDP price measure and retail inflation cover different things, so even the correct calculation is not a CPI estimate.
